title: UCL Master's Engineers Build a 150kg Bamboo Cargo Bike
body_html:
When you ask trained engineers to put bamboo under load, you stop guessing and start measuring. That is exactly what happened when Bamboo Bicycle Club ran a live design brief with Master's students at University College London.

The brief

Over a six-month project, UCL Master's students worked with Bamboo Bicycle Club to test the structural properties of bamboo and design a working cargo bike — one built to carry a **150kg load** for a low-resource farming context. Rather than treating bamboo as a curiosity, the brief asked students to approach it as a serious structural material and back every decision with data.

What we did

Bamboo Bicycle Club brought its frame-building craft — bamboo tube preparation and natural-fibre composite joinery — and the students brought formal engineering methodology. Together they tested how bamboo carries load, examined joint behaviour, and developed a cargo-bike design sized for a real-world carrying job rather than a lab demonstration.

The outcome

The students completed a working prototype grounded in their own structural testing — an evidence-based answer to a question BBC is asked often: can a natural material like bamboo really take the strain? It was an applied-engineering education project, not a commercial commission, and that is the point: BBC turns real design problems into real teaching.

In James's words

"Project with UCL, working with Master students on a 6-month project testing structural
properties and building a cargo bike to hold 150kg. Our education programme has grown and we
work with schools in the UK and abroad."
— James Marr, founder, Bamboo Bicycle Club

Why it matters

This is how Bamboo Bicycle Club's education work runs at university level: live, hands-on briefs where students design, build and test for themselves. It is the same ethos that drives BBC's school and workshop programmes — learning by making, with the evidence to back it up.
